'''Andrew Streitwieser''' was an American chemist known for his contributions to [[physical organic chemistry]].

Streitwieser was born in 1927 in [[Buffalo, New York]] and he grew up in [[New York City]].  He attended [[Columbia College, Columbia University|Columbia College]] and then [[Columbia University]] where he earned a PhD in the research group of [[William von Eggers Doering]] in  1952.<ref name=MSU>[https://www.chemistry.msu.edu/faculty-research/portraits/andrew-streitwieser-jr/ Michigan State University. Department of Chemistry. Portraits. Andrew Streitwieser, Jr.], retrieved Aug. 11, 2018.</ref> He then was a [[postdoctoral fellow]] in the laboratory of [[John D. Roberts]] at [[MIT]].  He has been Professor of Chemistry at the [[University of California, Berkeley]] since 1953.

Streitwieser was one of the pioneers of [[molecular orbital theory]] and his book ''Molecular Orbital Theory for Organic Chemists'' had a lasting impact on the field.<ref>{{cite web | title = Early Ideas in the History of Quantum Chemistry: Andrew Streitwieser | publisher = quantum-chemistry-history.com | url = http://www.quantum-chemistry-history.com/Streitw1.htm}}</ref>  He is also well-known for proposing the currently accepted interpretation of the origin of secondary deuterium [[kinetic isotope effect]]s.<ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Streitwieser|first1=A.|last2=Jagow|first2=R. H.|last3=Fahey|first3=R. C.|last4=Suzuki|first4=S.|date=May 1958|title=Kinetic Isotope Effects in the Acetolyses of Deuterated Cyclopentyl Tosylates1,2|journal=Journal of the American Chemical Society|language=EN|volume=80|issue=9|pages=2326–2332|doi=10.1021/ja01542a075|bibcode=1958JAChS..80.2326S |issn=0002-7863}}</ref>  Streitwieser developed the technique of using protium/deuterium exchange to measure the acidity of exceedingly weak carbon acids and was a codeveloper of the M'''S'''AD acidity scale, named for the first initials of the chemists who developed it.<ref>{{Cite book|title=Fundamentals of Carbanion Chemistry.|last=J.|first=Cram, Donald|date=1965|publisher=Elsevier Science|isbn=9780323162449|location=Burlington|oclc=843200178}}</ref>  His ''Chemical Reviews'' article titled "Solvolytic Displacement Reactions at Saturated Carbon"<ref>{{cite journal | title = Solvolytic Displacement Reactions At Saturated Carbon Atoms | author = Andrew Streitwieser Jr. | journal = Chem. Rev. | year = 1956 | volume = 56 | issue = 4 | pages = 571–752 | doi = 10.1021/cr50010a001}}</ref> was influential in the field of physical organic chemistry.  Streitwieser is also the author of the widely used university textbook ''Introduction to Organic Chemistry'' (4th revised ed., 1998, with [[Clayton Heathcock|Heathcock]] and [[Edward Kosower|Kosower]], {{ISBN|0139738509}}, German translation, ''Organische Chemie'', {{ISBN| 3527258108}}), as well as the autobiography ''A Lifetime of Synergy With Theory and Experiment'' ({{ISBN|0841218366}}).

Streitwieser was elected to the [[United States National Academy of Sciences]] in 1969 and was an [[American Chemical Society]] Fellow.  He is the recipient of the ACS Award in Petroleum Chemistry (1967), James Flack Norris Award in Physical Organic Chemistry (1982), the [[Guggenheim Fellowship]] (1968), the [[Arthur C. Cope]] Scholar Award (1989), and the Roger Adams Award (2009).<ref>{{cite web | url = http://chem.berkeley.edu/faculty/emeriti/streitwieser.php | publisher = Department of Chemistry, University of California, Berkeley | title = Emeritus Faculty, Andrew Streitwieser}}</ref>
